# Card 017 — US Army Intelligence Support Activity (ISA) at undivided commitment, attached to MACV-JSOC from September 1964, with eight cleared heritage Vietnamese interpreters

*Memorandum 017 · status part1 · full record: memos/017/ · generated by fie.py*

## P017a · US Army Intelligence Support Activity (USAISA, 'the Activity', Task Force Orange), in its 2026 configuration and at full strength: the whole unit committed to Vietnam, with its operations (clandestine human intelligence and close-target reconnaissance) squadron, its signals intelligence squadron, its mission support and communications squadron, its analysis, medical and logistics detachments and its small fleet of manned special-mission aircraft, attached to the MACV Joint Special Operations Command of memorandum 014 (P014b) to find targets for SFOD-D (P014a) and, second, for the combined task force against the infrastructure of memorandum 012 (P012b), MACV J-2 on request; without the wider JSOC package (no 160th SOAR, no dedicated JSOC drone wing, no national systems beyond the space_constellations condition); with eight TS/SCI-cleared heritage Vietnamese-speaking interpreters attached from arrival; across the borders only where and when history's forces went
the whole unit, undivided commitment [U]; ~360–440 personnel [E: open-source growth from about 100 in 1981 to a three-squadron unit with an aviation element and support detachments, D1], plus 8 TS/SCI-cleared heritage Vietnamese interpreters [U] · spaces ~370–450 [E: the whole unit and its eight interpreters; no ceiling (CONFIG troop_ceiling = NONE)] · arrives 1964-09-01 · FIND, SUBVERT, STRIKE, INTERDICT · isr

**Key figures.**
- Unit: Field Operations Group summer 1980, USAISA 3 March 1981, under JSOC from 2003; about 50 at founding, over 100 in 1981 [M017·S1] [M017·S2]
- In theater: about 360–440 people plus 8 TS/SCI heritage Vietnamese interpreters, from 1 September 1964, attached to MACV-JSOC [E: D1] [U]
- Organisation: operations (human intelligence) squadron 120–140, signals intelligence squadron 100–115, support and communications 65–75, aviation 35–45, headquarters and analysis 40–65 [E: D1]
- Aircraft: 4–6 King Air 350-class signals and imaging aircraft; 120–150 sorties a month; 250–400 useful fixes a month at maturity, falling as the enemy learns [E: D5]
- Fix accuracy 30–80 m with two aircraft, 100–300 m with one, against history's ARDF of several hundred metres to a kilometre; to the user in 10–20 minutes against hours [E: D4, D5]
- Sources: 40–60 by end 1964, 120–150 by end 1965, 200–240 by end 1967 [E: D5]
- Output at maturity: 15–25 raid-grade target packages a month, 20–30 close-target reconnaissances, 30–50 leads to the task force [E: D5]
- 2026 electronics stock about two to three years of wastage; thinning from 1966–67 [E: D8]
- History's benchmarks: ARDF from March 1962, 23 transmitters fixed in its first 162 missions [M017·S3]; 30 Army ARDF aircraft by 1965 and 41 more after Starlight [M017·S4]; the enemy's intercept network exposed on 20 December 1969 [M017·S5]

**Negative specification.** The Activity cannot hear what is not transmitted, and most of this enemy's command never touches the air: below COSVN, the regions and the main-force headquarters, the Front runs on couriers, wire and word of mouth [H]. Its 2026 craft was built against telephones; there are none here. It brings no national code-breaking: it locates and characterises transmitters, and reads only what the Army Security Agency or its own linguists can read [E: judgment from the open record and the period's practice]. A fix locates a radio, often on a hilltop away from the headquarters it serves; it never locates the battalions of a regiment under canopy (POS003-1). Its aircraft cannot see under triple canopy, cannot fly over the North, and stay above 20,000 feet over Laos [E: D7]. Its Americans cannot blend into a Vietnamese hamlet, and its eight heritage interpreters speak the Vietnamese of 2026, not the Party's [U] [E: judgment from the open record and the period's practice]. It has no authority to arrest, detain, interrogate or strike; it finds, and others act [M012] [M014]. It cannot cross a border before history's forces did, and nothing it hears in Cambodia can be acted on until 1967 on foot and 1969 from the air [M014]. Its electronics cannot be repaired or replaced in this war: two to three years of stock [E: D8]. It cannot be handed to the ARVN except as method (D9). And it is small: about 120–140 collectors, refilled at 25–35 a year [E: D2].

**Denies the enemy.** It denies the enemy's senior command the free use of radio. From late 1964 every transmission from a COSVN section, a region or a main-force headquarters can be fixed to 30–80 metres within minutes [E: D4], so the enemy must move his transmitters away from his commanders, shorten his schedules and fall silent before operations: slower command at every level that used radio. It denies the senior cadre in the towns and the held belt the safety of a cover identity, and it denies them the assumption that a raid needs months of file work: a package can be built in weeks. It denies COSVN in Cambodia the certainty that it is unlocated, though not that it is unreachable before 1969. It does not deny the enemy his couriers, his main force under canopy, his sanctuaries or his hamlets at night.

**Verdict.** The Activity is the finder the raid force lacked, and that matters. Delta could take a man from a guarded house at night; what it could not do was learn which house (F014-4). From late 1964 a small unit of about 400 recruits the drivers, merchants and relatives around the Front's senior cadre in the towns and the held belt, confirms what they say against the enemy's own radio, and gives MACV-JSOC a name, a place and a six-hour window, 15–25 times a month at maturity [E: D5]. That is perhaps 80–100 more senior cadre taken a year by 1967 and about twice that in 1965–66, which hastens the displacement of the Front's senior apparatus into Cambodia that the raid force had already begun (POS014-1). Its airborne fixes make history's direction finding five to ten times more precise and ten times faster, and that adds a point or two to the share of main-force contacts begun on a located unit [E: judgment from the open record and the period's practice]. It hears COSVN in Cambodia, which nothing else in the record does well, and that will matter when the bombing of the base areas opens in 1969. It is not a transformation. A unit built for an enemy who carries telephones meets an enemy who carries letters, and the war is decided in hamlets it cannot enter, by a main force it cannot see, from sanctuaries it can only listen to. The Activity makes the scalpel sharper and more accurate. It does not make it bigger.
